questions.query: In the course's feature-vector representation, what numeric type is used for each value?

questions.query: What does bucketing do to a numerical feature?
questions.proposed_answer: Bucketing, or binning, converts numerical values into buckets representing ranges.

questions.query: How can unequal feature scales slow gradient descent?
questions.proposed_answer: Different ranges can make gradient descent bounce, delaying convergence; normalization puts features on comparable scales.

questions.query: Why is a single NaN value dangerous inside a model?
questions.proposed_answer: A single NaN can propagate until other numbers in the model also become NaN.

questions.query: What does a Z-score of +2 say about an observation's distance above the average?
questions.proposed_answer: The observation is two standard deviations above the mean.

questions.query: What distribution and stability conditions make linear scaling a good choice?
questions.proposed_answer: Use linear scaling when bounds are stable, outliers are few and mild, and values are roughly uniform over the range.

questions.query: How does vocabulary encoding let a model treat categories differently?
questions.proposed_answer: It makes each category a separate feature so training can learn a different weight for each.

questions.query: What does a sparse one-hot representation store, and what form does the model train on?
questions.proposed_answer: Sparse storage records the nonzero position, but the model trains on the one-hot vector itself.

questions.query: What does the hashing trick map a category to?
questions.proposed_answer: It maps a category to a small integer identifying the bucket that will contain it.

questions.query: When can a small dataset still produce good results through model adaptation?
questions.proposed_answer: A small dataset can work when adapting a model already trained on much more data with the same schema.

questions.query: How does the course define dataset quality in practical terms?
questions.proposed_answer: High-quality data helps a model achieve its goal, while low-quality data obstructs that goal.

questions.query: How can an external formal schema help detect unreliable data automatically?
questions.proposed_answer: Unit tests based on a formal schema can flag feature values outside defined ranges.

questions.query: What extra metadata should accompany an imputed feature?
questions.proposed_answer: Add a Boolean column indicating whether each value of that feature was imputed.

questions.query: What determines whether a proxy label makes a useful model?
questions.proposed_answer: Its usefulness depends on how strongly the proxy label is connected to the prediction actually wanted.

questions.query: In the label lesson, when can a proxy be needed even though the desired direct label exists?
questions.proposed_answer: The lesson recommends a proxy when the desired direct label cannot be represented easily as a floating-point number in its modeling setup.

questions.query: What check does the lesson recommend for human-generated labels?
questions.proposed_answer: Label a sample yourself, compare it with raters' labels, and investigate discrepancies without assuming your own labels are correct.

questions.query: How does underfitting reveal itself on the training data?
questions.proposed_answer: An underfit model performs poorly even on its training examples.

questions.query: What two broad conditions cause overfitting according to the lesson?
questions.proposed_answer: Overfitting arises when training data does not represent real life or when the model is too complex.

questions.query: What do independence and stationarity require of training examples?
questions.proposed_answer: Examples must not influence each other, and the data-generating distribution should not change significantly over time.

questions.query: How can a recommendation model create a feedback loop in train-ticket prices?
questions.proposed_answer: Riders act on the recommendation, reducing available seats and causing the company to raise prices, so predictions alter the environment.

questions.query: Why can one large weight dominate an L2 complexity penalty?
questions.proposed_answer: L2 squares weights, so values near zero contribute little while a large weight can contribute most of total complexity.

questions.query: Does the lesson describe L2 as shrinking weights or as forcing them to exact zeros?
questions.proposed_answer: The lesson describes L2 as encouraging weights toward zero rather than forcing exact-zero weights.

Epochs

During training, an epoch means that the
model has processed every example in the training set once. For example, given
a training set with 1,000 examples and a mini-batch size of 100 examples, it
will take the model 10 iterations to
complete one epoch.

Training typically requires many epochs. That is, the system needs to process
every example in the training set multiple times.

The number of epochs is a hyperparameter you set before the model begins
training. In many cases, you'll need to experiment with how many epochs it takes
for the model to converge. In general, more epochs produces a better model, but
also takes more time to train.
